'''Andrew R. Barron''' (born 20 May 1962) is a British chemist, academic, and entrepreneur. He is the Sêr Cymru Chair of Low Carbon Energy and Environment at [[Swansea University]], and the Charles W. Duncan Jr.-Welch Foundation Chair in Chemistry at [[Rice University]].<ref name=SCIENCEMAG>{{Cite web|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/science-wales|title=Science in Wales|date=April 26, 2013|website=Science &#124; AAAS}}</ref> He is the founder and director of Energy Safety Research Institute (ESRI) at Swansea University,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.esri-swansea.org/en/|title=Welcome &#124; Energy Safety Research Institute (ESRI)|first=Waters Creative|last=Ltd (www.waters-creative.co.uk)|website=www.esri-swansea.org}}</ref> which consolidates the energy research at the University with a focus on environmental impact and future security.<ref name=EAEM>{{cite web|url=http://www.eaem.co.uk/news/new-super-filter-could-solve-fracking-water-pollution-problems|title=New super filter could solve fracking water pollution problems|access-date=2018-03-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626192404/http://www.eaem.co.uk/news/new-super-filter-could-solve-fracking-water-pollution-problems|archive-date=2018-06-26}}</ref> At Rice University, he leads a Research Group and has served as Associate Dean for Industry Interactions and Technology Transfer.<ref name=RICE3>{{Cite web|url=http://barron.rice.edu/Barron.html|title=Barron Research Group - Rice University - Andrew R. Barron|website=barron.rice.edu}}</ref>

Barron’s current focus is on implementation of economically viable [[Carbon capture and storage|carbon capture, utilization, and storage]] technology including [[Enhanced weathering|mineralization]] and biorefinery.<ref name="RICE3" /> He is a proponent of demonstrating new technologies through the concept of scaled pilots on industrial relevant locations, and in particular the concept of [[Technology readiness level|TRL]] jumping.<ref name="RICE" />

Most of Barron's work has revolved around the study of [[nanoparticles]] and their applications. Early on, he studied how the structure of a molecule could overcome thermodynamic control and create new solid state structures. Some of his early work also dealt with alumoxanes and [[Ceramic nanoparticle|ceramic nanomaterials]].<ref name=ACS2>{{cite journal|title= New Method for the Determination of the Trialkylaluminum Content in Alumoxanes|journal= Organometallics|volume= 14|issue= 7|pages= 3581–3583|doi= 10.1021/om00007a070|year = 1995|last1 = Barron|first1 = Andrew R.}}</ref> In the early 2000s, his research began to focus on carbon nanomaterials, the functionalization of [[fullerene]]s and single walled [[carbon nanotube]]s. Later, application of nanotechnology to energy problems became the focal point of his work. He has authored over 440 papers and 6 books, including a book co-authored with his wife, Merrie Barron, entitled ''Project Management for Scientists and Engineers''.<ref name=Archive>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/ost-engineering-col11120-14|title=Project Management for Scientists and Engineers|publisher=Connexions|year=2011}}</ref><ref name=THECONVERSATION>{{Cite web|url=https://theconversation.com/profiles/andrew-barron-444710|title=Andrew Barron|website=The Conversation|date=14 February 2018 }}</ref>

Barron is the co-founder of multiple companies<ref name="MEDIWALES">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mediwales.com/event/wales-festival-of-innovation-lessons-from-an-accidental-entrepreneur-prof-andrew-r-barron/|title=Wales Festival of Innovation: Lessons from an Accidental Entrepreneur - Prof Andrew R. Barron - MediWales|website=www.mediwales.com}}</ref> and he was a co-founder of the Rice Alliance.<ref name=RICE>{{Cite web|url=http://chemistry.rice.edu/FacultyDetail.aspx?RiceID=585|title=Charles W. Duncan, Jr. - Welch Chair of Chemistry & Professor of Materials Science & NanoEngineering|access-date=2018-03-30|archive-date=2018-03-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180330211813/http://chemistry.rice.edu/FacultyDetail.aspx?RiceID=585|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Barron has received several awards for his research and work. He was named one of the Top 100 Influential People in 2025,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Most Influential People of 2025 - Top 100 2025 Winners |url=https://top100influentialpeople.com/award_category/2025-winners/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=Top 100 Influential People |language=en-GB}}</ref> and is the recipient of the Star of Asia International Award (2019),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor wins international award for ongoing global collaborations |url=https://www.swansea.ac.uk/press-office/news-events/news/2019/09/professor-wins-international-award-for-ongoing-global-collaborations.php |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=Swansea University |language=en-GB}}</ref> and the first [[Welch Foundation]] Norman Hackerman Award in Chemical Research (2002). In 2011 Barron was awarded the World Technology Award for Materials,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Rice's Barron wins World Technology Award for Materials |url=https://news2.rice.edu/2011/10/27/rices-barron-wins-world-technology-award-for-materials/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=news2.rice.edu}}</ref> which is award by World Technology Network.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The World Technology Network |url=https://www.wtn.net/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=Untitled |language=en-US}}</ref> in association with [[Time (magazine)|TIME]], [[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]], [[CNN]], [[Science (journal)|Science]] magazine and [[MIT Technology Review|Technology Review]] across 20 categories for ‘innovative work of the greatest likely long-term significance’ to humanity. One of that year's fellow WTA Award winners was [[Steve Jobs]] for the [[iPhone]]. He is a fellow of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name=RSC>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/prizes-funding/prizes/prize-archive-hub/|title=Archive|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Barron was born in [[Welwyn Garden City]], and brought up in [[Farnham]], [[Surrey]], where he attended [[Farnham Heath End School|Heath End School]] and [[Farnham College|Farnham Sixth Form College]]. In 1983, Barron completed his BSc in chemistry from [[Imperial College]]. Subsequently, he received his PhD degree in 1986 from Imperial College under the supervision of [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]].<ref name="RSC" />

After completing his PhD, Barron moved to the [[United States]] and joined [[University of Texas at Austin]] for his post-doctoral research, which dealt with the chemistry of multiple bonds to phosphorus and carbon. He published the first [[Characterization (materials science)|structural characterization]] of a CP triple bond in 1988 in a paper he co-authored with [[Alan Cowley]].<ref name="RSC2">{{cite journal |last1=Barron |first1=Andrew R. |last2=Hall |first2=Stephen W. |last3=Cowley |first3=Alan H. |year=1987 |title=Cyclic carboxylic monophosphides: a new class of phosphorus heterocycle |journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications |issue=23 |pages=1753–1754 |doi=10.1039/C39870001753}}</ref> In 1987, he joined [[Harvard University]] as an assistant professor of chemistry and was promoted to associate professor in 1991.<ref name="BIZJOURNALS">{{cite web |title=New solar energy firm launches, heats competition |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/boston/blog/mass-high-tech/2007/10/new-solar-energy-firm-launches-heats.html}}</ref>

== Later career ==
Barron left [[Harvard University]] in 1995, when he joined Rice University as professor of Chemistry and Materials Science. He stepped down from his position at Gallia in 1997. In 1998, he was appointed as the Charles W. Duncan Jr.-Welch Foundation Chair in Chemistry at Rice University.<ref name=RICE2>{{Cite web|url=http://barron.rice.edu/arb_full_CV_2012.pdf|title=Andrew R. Barron}}</ref>

Following his studies on ceramic nanoparticles and the discovery of their applications, he founded Oxane Materials in 2002. The company developed nanoproducts with applications in the field of energy.<ref name=BIZJOURNALS2>{{cite web|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/houston/print-edition/2013/03/15/how-oxane-materials-chris-coker.html |title= How Oxane Materials' Chris Coker thought small to make it big}}</ref> Building on his research with nanoparticles, Barron founded Natcore Technology in 2004 and joined the scientific advisory board of the company. The company manufactures nanoparticles and technology with applications in the solar sectors.<ref name=INSIDER>{{cite web|title=Natcore Technology Inc (OTCMKTS:NTCXF) Unveils Its Latest Solar Technology|url= https://insiderfinancial.com/natcore-technology-inc-otcmktsntcxf-unveils-its-latest-solar-technology|date= 2018-03-23}}</ref>

From 2006 to 2008, he served as the Associate Dean of Industry Interactions and Technology Transfer at the Rice University. In 2019 he was appointed as the Prince of Wales Visiting Innovator with an appointment at the [[University of Wales]].<ref name="RICE2" /> In 2013 he was appointed as the Sêr Cymru Chair of Low Carbon Energy and Environment, [[Swansea University]]. His research in the field of energy and environment resulted in his foundation of the Energy Safety Research Institute (ESRI), with the vision of "building the bridge to a sustainable, affordable and secure energy future." ESRI was housed in the first [[BREEAM]] Outstanding Building in Wales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Energy Safety Research Institute (ESRI) |url=https://stridetreglown.com/projects/the-energy-safety-research-institute-esri-swansea-university/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=Stride Treglown |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Barron is the editor of Journal of Nanomaterials since 2013<ref name=HINDWAI>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hindawi.com/journals/jnm/editors/|title=jnm - Editorial Board|website=Hindawi}}</ref> and [[Scientific Reports]] since 2014.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/srep/about/editorial-board |title=Editorial Advisory Panel and Editorial Board}}</ref> He is also part of the editorial boards of Main Group Chemistry and Materials Science in Semiconductor Processing. Barron has served on the advisory board of [[King Abdullah University of Science and Technology]], Zhu Zhou International Research Institute China, and Yellow River Delta Efficient Eco-economic Development.<ref name=RICE/>

== Research ==
=== Molecular control over solid state structure ===
In the early 1990s, Barron developed interest in studying how the structure of a molecule could overcome thermodynamic control and create new solid state structures. As such, he synthesized a class of cubic [[Gallium]] [[chalcogenide]] compounds and showed that a new meta-stable phase could be synthesized.<ref name=ACS>{{cite journal|title= Synthesis of Gallium Chalcogenide Cubanes and Their Use as CVD Precursors for Ga2E3 (E = S, Se)|journal= Organometallics|volume= 15|issue= 22|pages= 4880–4883|doi= 10.1021/om960480w|year = 1996|last1 = Schulz|first1 = Stephan|last2= Gillan|first2= Edward G.|last3= Ross|first3= Jean L.|last4= Rogers|first4= Lillian M.|last5= Rogers|first5= Robin D.|last6= Barron|first6= Andrew R.}}</ref>

=== Alumoxanes ===
Following from his work on the chalcogenides, Barron was the first person to [[Crystallography|crystallographically]] characterize an [[Methylaluminoxane|alkylalumoxane]] in 1993. These structures were [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopically]] consistent with methylalumoxane and he showed that despite being octet molecules they had significant [[Lewis acids and bases|Lewis acidity]], he termed this as "Latent Lewis acidity", and showed that this mechanism applied to a number of MAO style polymerization systems. Barron's 3-dimensional model has been evolved by others but is essentially the same as now widely accepted.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Andrew R. Barron |date=July 1995 |title=New Method for the Determination of the Trialkylaluminum Content in Alumoxanes |journal=Organometallics |volume=14 |issue=7 |pages=3581–3583 |doi=10.1021/om00007a070 |s2cid=33271800}}</ref>

=== Ceramic nanomaterials ===
While investigating MAO-like structures, Barron noticed the relationship between clusters and minerals, at the same time he became interested in metalloxane polymers. He determined that these "polymers" were actually [[nanoparticle]]s. Furthermore, he showed that these metal oxide nanoparticles could be chemically made by a top-down approach from minerals with which they shared their structures. With the ability to make a range of nanoparticles with different functional groups and control over size, Barron found that the structure and physical properties of macroscopic materials could be controlled by alterations at the [[Nanoscopic scale|nanometer scale]].<ref>{{cite journal|title= Strengthening of porous alumina bodies using carboxylate-alumoxane nanoparticles|journal= Journal of Materials Science|volume= 38|issue= 5|pages= 927–935|doi= 10.1023/A:1022364822978|year = 2003|last1 = Defriend|first1 = Kimberly A.|last2= Barron|first2= Andrew R.|s2cid= 134080915}}</ref>

Barron was the first to discover that nanoparticle derived ceramics could be designed to have intra-granular [[porosity]], meaning that the pores are within the crystal grain rather than between the crystal grains as normally observed. This had implications in composites and in membranes and separation processes. Through his research, Barron developed a process that forms hollow spheres of ceramic with exceptional crush strength.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A flexible route to high strength α-alumina and aluminate spheres|journal=Journal of Materials Science|volume=38|issue=12|pages=2673–2678|doi=10.1023/A:1024494821196|year = 2003|last1 = Defriend|first1 = Kimberly A.|last2=Barron|first2=Andrew R.|s2cid=133915657}}</ref>

Barron rationalized that if hollow ceramic spheres could be made on a large scale, they could replace dense ceramics being used in oil extraction and minimize waste. He created a spin-off company to commercialize this technology.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Enhanced oil recovery method developed |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2017/07/170719100524.htm |website=ScienceDaily}}</ref> In 2010, Barron and his team, on the request of U.S. Navy, developed a ceramic membrane with microscale pores that could filter out [[virus]] contaminants from waters and protect divers, which was later applied to [[COVID-19]] PPE, and also the basis of a process to separate hydrocarbon out of [[produced water]].<ref>{{cite web |date=2017-09-26 |title=Swansea filter could help reduce environmental impact of fracking |url=https://www.theengineer.co.uk/swansea-filter-fracking/}}</ref>

=== Carbon nanomaterials ===
Barron investigated the impact of a fullerene on wide range of systems. Initial work was concerned with the toxicity on various cell types. The results of this work demonstrated that inclusion of C<sub>60</sub> into a [[peptide]] structure drastically lowered any toxicity effects.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rouse |first1=Jillian G. |last2=Yang |first2=Jianzhong |last3=Ryman-Rasmussen |first3=Jessica P. |last4=Barron |first4=Andrew R. |last5=Monteiro-Riviere |first5=Nancy A. |author-link5=Nancy A. Monteiro-Riviere |year=2007 |title=Effects of Mechanical Flexion on the Penetration of Fullerene Amino Acid-Derivatized Peptide Nanoparticles through Skin |journal=Nano Letters |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=155–160 |bibcode=2007NanoL...7..155R |doi=10.1021/nl062464m |pmid=17212456}}</ref>

In his later work, Barron studied catalysis with growth of single walled [[carbon nanotube]]s (SWCNTs) pioneering the concept of amplification of a CNT.<ref>{{cite journal|title= Amplification of Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes from Designed Seeds: Separation of Nucleation and Growth|journal= The Journal of Physical Chemistry C|volume= 111|issue= 48|pages= 17804–17806|doi= 10.1021/jp0712506|year = 2007|last1 = Ogrin|first1 = Douglas|last2= Anderson|first2= Robin E.|last3= Colorado|first3= Ramon|last4= Maruyama|first4= Benji|last5= Pender|first5= Mark J.|last6= Moore|first6= Valerie C.|last7= Pheasant|first7= Sean T.|last8= McJilton|first8= Laura|last9= Schmidt|first9= Howard K.|last10= Hauge|first10= Robert H.|last11= Billups|first11= W. Edward|last12= Tour|first12= James M.|last13= Smalley|first13= Richard E.|last14= Barron|first14= Andrew R.|url= https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/2970328|url-access= subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/01/180103101102.htm|title=Carbon nanotubes devices may have a limit to how 'nano' they can be: Energy Safety Research Institute shows decontaminating nanotubes can simplify nanoscale devices|website=ScienceDaily}}</ref> Other work includes measuring electrical properties of individual CNTs,<ref name="sciencedaily.com">{{Cite web |title=Carbon nanotubes devices may have a limit to how &apos;nano&apos; they can be |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/01/180103101102.htm |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=ScienceDaily |language=en}}</ref> and using them to absorbs cadmium, cobalt, copper, mercury, nickel and lead from contaminated water.<ref name="sciencedaily.com"/>

=== Environmental research ===
In the mid 2010s, Barron returned to the issue of water purification. He has investigated the nano control over the surface of a material that allows for the creation of [[Superhydrophilicity|superhydrophilic]] surfaces that allow for separation of oil and water without fouling.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.engineering.com/story/carbon-nanotube-filter-removes-over-99-of-heavy-metal-toxins-from-water|title=Carbon Nanotube Filter Removes Over 99% of Heavy Metal Toxins from Water by Staff|website=Engineering.com}}</ref> In this area, his research focused on energy problems including sustainable resources and waste recovery, reducing the impact of hydrocarbon energy sources, carbon dioxide valorisation and long-term sequestration and the next generation of the energy distribution.<ref name=RICE/>

== Entrepreneurship ==
Barron is a serial entrepreneur.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-01-01 |title=Prof. Andrew Barron's Green Tech Revolution |url=https://www.allaroundworlds.com/journey-of-prof-andrew-r-barron/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=All Around Worlds |language=en}}</ref> In 1992 whilst at Harvard University, Barron founded Gallia Inc. that was sold to [[TriQuint Semiconductor]] in 1995. In 2001 Barron co-founded a Rice University spin-out to develop silicon solar cell technologies, Natcore technology, which was coincidentally founded on [[September 11 attacks|9/11]]. Oxane Materials was set up for the commercialization of nano-technology-enhanced propping agents that addressed critical oil and gas technical challenges.Based upon the superhydrophilic functionality of ceramic membranes, Apex Water Solutions was founded in 2019 to implement large scale water treatment for the energy industry.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Apex – Water Treatment Solutions |url=https://apexws.com/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2019, Apex Water Solutions was founded to develop large-scale water treatment systems for the energy industry based on [[Superhydrophilicity|superhydrophilic]] ceramic membrane technology. The same membrane functionality was later applied in the development of FXI Inc.’s antiviral X-mask personal protective equipment.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Red Dot Design Award: X-Mask |url=https://www.red-dot.org/project/x-mask-71801 |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=www.red-dot.org}}</ref>

MiDAS Green Innovations was established in 2019 to coordinate multiple technologies related to industrial decarbonization, including carbon capture, utilization, and sequestration.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-12 |title=Inside the Vision of MiDAS Green Innovations: An Exclusive Interview with Prof. Andrew Barron |url=https://xraised.com/videos/inside-the-vision-of-midas-green-innovations-an-exclusive-interview-with-prof-andrew-barron/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |website=xraised |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Barron lives with his wife, Merrie Barron, in both Swansea (Wales) and Houston (Texas). Since he moved to Texas in the 1990s, he has participated in motor racing as a sport. In 1999 American Lemans Series, he was team principle for team in the GTS class. He participated in the final season of USRRC under Ross Racing. Barron has previously raced Lotus Seven, Caterham Seven, and Lotus Type 61 Formula Ford. He has been SW Division SCCA E-Production Champion, 2013 Monoposto Formula Ford Champion,<ref>{{cite web|title= Monoposto Wraps up Another Exciting Championship Season|url= http://www.monoposto.com/MR_News.html|access-date= 2018-03-30|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190116052413/http://www.monoposto.com/MR_News.html|archive-date= 2019-01-16}}</ref> 2013 SVRA Group 2 Sprint Series Champion and 2014 Monoposto Formula Ford Champion.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.monoposto.com/MR_News.html |title=Final 2014 Monoposto Championship Results |access-date=2018-03-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190116052413/http://www.monoposto.com/MR_News.html |archive-date=2019-01-16 }}</ref> In 2018, he raced FIA Formula Opel Racing with a Formula Vauxhall Lotus.<ref name=RICE/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.arbmotorsports.com/|title=ARB Motorsports United Kingdom|website=arbmotorsports}}</ref>
